**Fraud detection is a decision under asymmetric costs.** Missing a fraudulent payment causes loss; declining a legitimate payment causes customer friction and lost revenue; manual review costs time and has limited capacity. The model score is only an input to choosing among approve, review, and decline.

**Why accuracy is misleading.** At 0.02% fraud prevalence, approving everything achieves 99.98% classification accuracy while detecting no fraud. Evaluate precision/recall at operational thresholds, expected financial loss, false declines, and review workload. Probabilities must be calibrated at realistic prevalence if they enter expected-cost calculations. [3](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html)

**Keep the authorization path short.** Precompute velocity counters and account/device aggregates, cache expensive graph features, and fetch them with bounded parallel requests. Traversing a large graph during every payment can violate a sub-50ms budget. The system needs a risk-tiered fallback for missing data rather than always approving or always declining.

**Labels arrive late and selectively.** Chargebacks may take weeks; reviewed transactions are not a random sample of all payments. Log review selection and outcome maturity. Treating all unreviewed or recent transactions as confirmed legitimate can bias training and evaluation.

Monitor new fraud patterns, feature drift, subgroup false declines, and queue delays. Deploy a challenger carefully with rollback. The goal is an effective decision policy under real constraints, not a model that maximizes one offline score while overwhelming reviewers or rejecting legitimate customers.

**Technical details and references.**

Start with a loss matrix: expected fraud loss, false-decline cost, review cost, and customer friction. At 0.02% prevalence, raw accuracy is useless; evaluate precision/recall and expected loss at the operational review/decline thresholds, then calibrate probabilities on representative prevalence.

A sub-50ms path should use precomputed velocity counters, device/account aggregates, and cached graph-risk features. Fetch them with parallel bounded calls, not an unbounded graph traversal at authorization time. Deduplicate payment events and distinguish event time from ingestion time. A fallback policy for missing features should be explicitly risk-tiered, not universally approve or decline.

Train on chargebacks and confirmed reviews with delay-aware labels. Review outcomes are selectively observed, so log selection and retain controlled audits where feasible. A review queue needs capacity-aware prioritization and SLA monitoring. Track fraud tactics, feature drift, false declines by cohort, and model calibration; use champion/challenger deployment and rapid rollback. Treat external features and identity signals as sensitive, access-controlled data.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** For a simple approve/decline choice, decline when predicted expected fraud loss exceeds expected false-decline and intervention cost, using a validated cost model. At very low prevalence, precision depends heavily on false positives and calibration. Include review capacity as a constraint, and test delayed labels and missing-feature fallback behavior before deploying a threshold. [3](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html)
